subject: Chemistry
title: Cadmium: The Itai-Itai Disease
description: One-minute skill: Cadmium: The Itai-Itai Disease.

hook.text: In 1950s Japan, villagers along the Jinzu River developed bones so weak they broke from coughing.

buildup.text: A nearby zinc mine dumped cadmium into the river. Rice paddies absorbed it; people ate contaminated rice for decades.

discovery.text: Cadmium replaces calcium in bones and blocks kidney function. Calcium leaches out, making bones brittle.

twist.text: Victims cried 'itai-itai' (ouch-ouch) from the pain. It became one of Japan's four major pollution diseases.

climax.text: Cadmium is still in rechargeable batteries and cigarette smoke. Smokers have twice the cadmium levels of non-smokers.

punchline.text: A metal that steals calcium from bones. Industry's hidden poison.

quiz.question: What caused itai-itai disease in Japan?
options: Cadmium from mining contaminated rice and replaced calcium in bones
Lead in drinking water damaged the nervous system
Mercury in fish accumulated in bone marrow

details.summary: Cadmium poisoning in the Toyama Prefecture of Japan caused itai-itai disease, characterized by extreme bone pain and skeletal deformities. Mining runoff contaminated rice paddies, and chronic dietary cadmium intake caused kidney damage that led to catastrophic calcium loss from bones.
details.whyItMatters: Itai-itai disease was one of the four major pollution-related diseases in Japan and catalyzed the development of environmental pollution regulations in the 1960s and 1970s.
takeaways: Cadmium replaces calcium in bones, causing severe weakening and pain
Mining runoff contaminated rice paddies in Toyama, Japan
The disease catalyzed Japan's landmark pollution control legislation

faq.question: Why does cadmium specifically target bones and kidneys?
faq.answer: Cadmium accumulates in kidneys because it binds to metallothionein proteins there. Kidney damage impairs vitamin D activation and calcium reabsorption. The resulting calcium deficiency causes the body to leach calcium from bones, leading to osteomalacia and spontaneous fractures.

faq.question: Is cadmium exposure still a concern in modern industrial settings?
faq.answer: Yes. Workers in battery manufacturing, electroplating, pigment production, and metal smelting face cadmium inhalation risks. Cigarette smoke is also a significant cadmium source. Regulatory limits have reduced exposure, but monitoring remains essential in these industries.
